english_text: BCG should not be given to HIV-positive infants with symptomatic HIV disease.
BCG vaccination can cause a false positive tuberculin skin test result.
BCG dissemination is a rare but serious complication of BCG vaccination in immunocompromised children.
New TB vaccines with better efficacy than BCG are urgently needed to control the global TB epidemic.
Latent TB infection (LTBI) means TB bacteria are present in the body but are not causing active disease.
An estimated 1.7 billion people — about one quarter of the world's population — have latent TB infection.
People with latent TB infection have a 5 to 10% lifetime risk of developing active TB disease.
The risk of LTBI progressing to active TB is highest in the first two years after infection.
Latent TB infection has no symptoms and is not infectious.
LTBI is diagnosed using the tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay.
Treatment of LTBI prevents progression to active TB disease.
LTBI treatment is recommended for HIV-positive people, recent TB contacts, and other high-risk groups.
Systematic testing and treatment of LTBI in high-risk groups is a key component of the End TB Strategy.
LTBI treatment uptake remains low globally due to lack of awareness, testing capacity, and drug availability.
TB prevention requires a combination of vaccination, infection control, treatment of latent infection, and addressing social determinants.
Improving living conditions, reducing overcrowding, and addressing poverty are essential for TB prevention.
Adequate nutrition reduces TB risk by supporting immune function.
Smoking cessation reduces TB risk and improves TB treatment outcomes.
Reducing alcohol consumption lowers TB risk and improves treatment adherence.
Good ventilation in homes and public spaces is a simple and effective TB prevention measure.
Spending time outdoors in sunlight and fresh air reduces TB transmission risk.
Early diagnosis and treatment of active TB is the most effective way to prevent TB transmission.
Universal health coverage ensures that all people can access TB prevention and treatment services.
TB prevention is everyone's responsibility — communities, governments, and health workers all have a role.
Prisoners have TB rates up to 23 times higher than the general population.
TB control in prisons requires screening on entry, treatment, and infection control measures.
Continuity of TB treatment for prisoners upon release is essential to prevent treatment interruption.
Mineworkers have among the highest TB rates of any occupational group globally.
Occupational health programmes for miners should include regular TB screening and treatment.
Dust suppression and improved ventilation in mines reduces silica exposure and TB risk.
Migrants face barriers to TB care including language differences, legal status, and lack of documentation.
TB services should be accessible to all people regardless of nationality or immigration status.
Homeless people with TB require integrated support including housing, nutrition, and social services.
People who use drugs are at high risk of TB and require harm reduction services alongside TB care.
Alcohol use disorder is associated with TB and requires integrated management.
Refugees living in camps are at high risk of TB due to overcrowding and limited healthcare access.
TB programmes must reach all key populations to achieve the End TB targets.
Stigma and discrimination prevent key populations from accessing TB services.
Community-led TB services improve access and trust among marginalised populations.
Children under five years are at the highest risk of severe TB disease after infection.
An estimated one million children develop TB disease each year globally.
TB in children is often missed because symptoms overlap with other common childhood illnesses.
Children with TB are usually infected by an adult with active TB in their household.
TB preventive therapy should be given to all child contacts of TB cases under five years of age.
BCG vaccination at birth significantly reduces the risk of TB meningitis and miliary TB in infants.
Paediatric TB diagnosis requires a combination of clinical assessment, history of TB contact, and diagnostic tests.
TB in adolescents often resembles adult pulmonary TB with cavitary disease.
School attendance and educational continuity should be supported for children on TB treatment.
Child-friendly TB services reduce fear and improve treatment adherence in young patients.
The WHO End TB Strategy has three pillars: integrated patient-centred care, bold policies, and intensified research.
Universal health coverage is a prerequisite for achieving the End TB targets.
TB notification data is used to monitor trends and guide national TB programme planning.
The political commitment of governments is essential for funding and implementing effective TB programmes.
Civil society organisations play a critical role in TB advocacy, community mobilisation, and service delivery.
TB survivors and affected communities must be meaningfully involved in TB policy and programme design.
Domestic financing for TB programmes must increase to reduce dependence on donor funding.
The Stop TB Partnership coordinates global TB efforts and advocates for increased resources.
The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria is a major funder of TB programmes worldwide.
TB is a notifiable disease in most countries, requiring healthcare providers to report all cases to health authorities.
Nurses are the backbone of TB care, providing diagnosis support, treatment initiation, and patient education.
Community health workers extend TB services to patients who cannot regularly attend health facilities.
Home visits by community health workers improve TB treatment adherence and reduce loss to follow-up.
TB patient education should cover disease transmission, treatment duration, side effects, and the importance of adherence.
Counselling at TB diagnosis should address fears, stigma, and the patient's support network.
TB treatment literacy empowers patients to understand their treatment and advocate for their own care.
TB support groups provide emotional support and practical advice for patients on treatment.
Defaulter tracing — following up patients who miss appointments — is a critical nursing responsibility.
TB registers must be accurately maintained to track patient outcomes and programme performance.
Infection control training for all health facility staff reduces occupational TB risk.
TB patients should receive nutritional assessment and counselling at the start of treatment.
Weight gain during TB treatment is a positive indicator of treatment response.
Energy and protein requirements are increased in TB patients due to the metabolic demands of infection.
Micronutrient supplementation including zinc, vitamin D, and vitamin A may support TB treatment outcomes.
Food insecurity is a major barrier to TB treatment adherence and should be addressed through social support.
TB patients who are severely malnourished may require therapeutic feeding alongside TB treatment.
Vitamin D deficiency is common in TB patients and may impair immune function.
Alcohol and TB have a bidirectional relationship — alcohol worsens TB and TB worsens alcohol use.
Nutritional support programmes for TB patients improve treatment completion rates.
A balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and protein supports recovery from TB.
Depression is common in TB patients and is associated with poor treatment adherence.
Anxiety about TB diagnosis, treatment side effects, and social consequences is common.
Screening for depression and anxiety should be integrated into TB care.
Psychosocial support improves mental health outcomes and treatment adherence in TB patients.
TB patients with mental health disorders require integrated care addressing both conditions.
The social isolation experienced by TB patients can worsen mental health and reduce quality of life.
Peer support from TB survivors can reduce stigma and improve mental health in newly diagnosed patients.
Healthcare workers caring for TB patients are at risk of burnout and compassion fatigue.
Cognitive impairment can occur in TB meningitis survivors and requires rehabilitation support.
Post-traumatic stress disorder has been reported in MDR-TB survivors following prolonged treatment.
I did not know that TB could be prevented — I wish someone had told me earlier.
After I recovered from TB, I started opening my windows every day to keep the air fresh.
I cover my mouth when I cough now, even when I am healthy, because I know how TB spreads.
My child received the BCG injection at birth and I am glad the nurse explained what it was for.
I was tested for latent TB because my husband had active TB, and I was given tablets to prevent it.
Living with TB taught me to take care of my health and not ignore symptoms.
I tell everyone in my community that TB is curable — there is no need to be ashamed.
After completing TB treatment, I felt stronger and more grateful for my health than ever before.
I joined a TB support group and met others who understood exactly what I was going through.
My faith helped me stay strong during my TB treatment journey.
I now volunteer at the clinic to support other TB patients the way I was supported.
TB changed my life, but it also made me stronger and more compassionate towards others who are sick.
I am proud that I never missed a single dose of my TB medication.
My doctor told me my lungs have healed well and I can live a normal life.
I want other people to know that TB is not a death sentence — you can recover and live fully.
The hardest part was telling my children I had TB, but they were very supportive.
I eat better now than before I had TB because I learned how important nutrition is.
I still get tired easily since finishing TB treatment, but the clinic says this will improve over time.
I was scared to go back to work after TB, but my employer was understanding.
Every day I am healthy is a gift — TB taught me not to take my health for granted.
A persistent cough lasting more than two weeks may be a sign of tuberculosis.
Night sweats that soak your clothes can be a symptom of active TB disease.
Unexplained weight loss is one of the classic warning signs of tuberculosis.
Coughing up blood or blood-stained sputum requires immediate medical attention.
Chest pain when breathing or coughing can indicate tuberculosis affecting the lungs.
Fatigue and general weakness are common early symptoms of tuberculosis.
A low-grade fever that persists for weeks can be a sign of TB infection.
Loss of appetite is frequently reported by patients with active tuberculosis.
Swollen lymph nodes in the neck can indicate extrapulmonary tuberculosis.
TB can affect organs other than the lungs, including the kidneys, spine, and brain.
A sputum smear test is one of the most common ways to diagnose pulmonary tuberculosis.
GeneXpert is a rapid molecular test that can detect TB and rifampicin resistance within two hours.
A chest X-ray can show changes in the lungs that suggest tuberculosis.
The tuberculin skin test, also called the Mantoux test, checks for TB infection.
A positive TB skin test does not always mean you have active TB disease.
Interferon-gamma release assays are blood tests used to diagnose latent TB infection.
Drug susceptibility testing helps determine which TB medicines will work for your infection.
Early diagnosis of tuberculosis is essential to prevent spread to others.
TB diagnosis in children can be challenging because they may not produce sputum easily.
Contact tracing helps identify people who may have been exposed to TB.
Standard TB treatment for drug-sensitive TB lasts six months.
The first two months of TB treatment use four drugs: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
The continuation phase of TB treatment uses isoniazid and rifampicin for four months.
Never stop taking your TB medication without consulting your healthcare provider.
Fixed-dose combination tablets make it easier to take all TB medicines at once.
TB medicines should be taken on an empty stomach for better absorption.
Rifampicin can turn your urine, sweat, and tears orange — this is normal and harmless.
Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy; vitamin B6 supplements help prevent this.
Pyrazinamide can cause joint pain and elevated uric acid levels.
Ethambutol can affect vision; report any changes in eyesight to your doctor immediately.
Liver toxicity is a serious side effect of some TB medicines; avoid alcohol during treatment.
Directly Observed Treatment ensures a healthcare worker watches you take each dose.
Video-observed therapy allows patients to take their TB medication at home via video call.
Treatment supporters can be family members, community health workers, or clinic staff.
Nutritional support during TB treatment improves treatment outcomes.
Patients with TB and diabetes need careful monitoring as both conditions affect each other.
Pregnant women with TB can be safely treated; discuss the safest regimen with your doctor.
Children with TB are treated with the same drugs as adults but at weight-adjusted doses.
TB treatment is free at all public health facilities in South Africa.
Drug-resistant TB develops when TB bacteria survive despite antibiotic treatment.
Multidrug-resistant TB is resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin.
Extensively drug-resistant TB is resistant to more TB medicines and is harder to treat.
MDR-TB treatment can last 9 to 20 months depending on the regimen used.
The BPaL regimen uses bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid for highly resistant TB.
Bedaquiline is a newer TB drug that works differently from older TB medicines.
Delamanid is another newer drug used in the treatment of drug-resistant TB.
Drug-resistant TB requires treatment at a specialised TB facility.
Incomplete treatment of drug-sensitive TB is the main cause of drug resistance.
Regular sputum cultures during MDR-TB treatment monitor your response to therapy.
The BCG vaccine protects infants and young children from severe forms of tuberculosis.
BCG vaccination is given at birth as part of the routine childhood immunisation schedule.
TB preventive therapy reduces the risk of latent TB progressing to active disease.
Isoniazid preventive therapy for six months is recommended for people living with HIV.
A three-month course of weekly isoniazid and rifapentine is an effective TB preventive regimen.
Ventilating indoor spaces reduces the concentration of TB bacteria in the air.
Opening windows and doors allows fresh air to dilute infectious TB particles.
Healthcare workers should wear N95 respirators when caring for TB patients.
UV germicidal irradiation can kill TB bacteria in indoor air.
Cough hygiene — covering your mouth when coughing — helps prevent TB transmission.
Treating latent TB infection is an important strategy for eliminating tuberculosis.
Household contacts of TB patients should be screened for TB infection.
Children under five who are household contacts of TB patients should receive TB preventive therapy.
Good nutrition strengthens the immune system and reduces the risk of developing active TB.
Reducing overcrowding in homes and workplaces lowers the risk of TB transmission.
Smoking increases the risk of developing active tuberculosis.
Alcohol use weakens the immune system and increases TB risk.
Diabetes mellitus triples the risk of developing active tuberculosis.
Malnutrition is the single largest risk factor for tuberculosis globally.
HIV is the strongest known risk factor for developing active tuberculosis.
The WHO four-symptom TB screen asks about cough, fever, weight loss, and night sweats.
People living with HIV who have TB symptoms should be tested with GeneXpert.
TB treatment should be started as soon as possible in people living with HIV.
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome can occur when ART is started during TB treatment.
Drug interactions between TB medicines and antiretrovirals require careful management.
Rifampicin reduces the blood levels of many antiretroviral drugs.
Efavirenz-based ART is preferred when treating TB and HIV simultaneously.
Integrated TB and HIV services improve patient outcomes and reduce loss to follow-up.
TB preventive therapy is recommended for all people living with HIV who do not have active TB.
Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis reduces the risk of opportunistic infections in TB-HIV patients.
Children with TB often have different symptoms than adults, including failure to thrive.
Adolescents with TB may feel stigmatised and need psychosocial support.
Older adults with TB may have atypical symptoms that delay diagnosis.
Prisoners and detainees are at high risk of TB due to overcrowding and poor ventilation.
Miners are at high risk of TB due to silica dust exposure and underground conditions.
Silicosis from mining dramatically increases the risk of developing tuberculosis.
Homeless people face significant barriers to TB diagnosis and treatment completion.
Migrants and refugees may have higher rates of TB and face barriers to healthcare access.
Healthcare workers are at increased risk of TB exposure and should be regularly screened.
TB screening programmes in high-risk workplaces save lives and reduce transmission.
TB stigma can prevent people from seeking diagnosis and completing treatment.
Tuberculosis is a disease, not a sign of weakness or moral failure.
